title: LinkedIn Ghostwriting Pricing: What B2B Founders Should Compare
summary: Compare LinkedIn ghostwriting proposals by source capture, deliverables, approval, and ownership instead of treating a monthly price as the whole scope.
body_markdown:
## Start with the work behind the price


LinkedIn ghostwriting pricing is easier to evaluate when a founder compares the operating work behind each proposal, not only the monthly number. A lower fee can describe a focused writing service. A higher fee can include source interviews, editorial direction, reviews, and distribution support. Neither is automatically the right choice.


The useful question is: what must happen for your experience to become accurate, useful LinkedIn content that still sounds like you? Once that workflow is visible, you can compare proposals without asking a vague price question to a vague service.


This guide is for B2B founders who are deciding whether a ghostwriting partner fits their current stage. It does not give a universal price range because scope, cadence, source material, and approval needs vary too much for a generic number to make a sound buying decision.


## Separate writing from the rest of the content system


A proposal that says it includes posts may mean several different things. It may cover drafting from notes you provide. It may include interviews to capture your experience. It may include strategy, planning, revisions, scheduling, or support after a post goes live. Compare those pieces directly.


Rethoric's[LinkedIn ghostwriting overview](https://www.rethoric.com/linkedin-ghostwriting-for-founders) describes founder interviews as an input to the writing process. That distinction matters: a writer cannot reliably preserve a founder's perspective if the source process is unclear.


Ask each provider to describe where their work begins and ends. A clear answer makes it easier to see whether you are buying drafting capacity, a managed editorial workflow, or a broader LinkedIn program.


## Compare the source-capture process


Source capture is the work that turns a founder's lived experience into material a writer can use. It might involve interviews, product notes, sales themes, customer questions, or a short voice memo. The right method depends on how much time you can give and how complex your subject matter is.


Before comparing prices, ask:


-


Who leads the source conversation, and how often does it happen?


-


What preparation is expected from the founder or internal team?


-


How are factual uncertainty and confidential details handled?


-


Can the provider work from your existing material without flattening your point of view?


A hypothetical example: one proposal includes four drafts from a founder's written notes. Another includes a monthly interview, an editorial brief, and four drafts. The comparison is not four posts versus four posts. It is two different ways of finding and shaping the material.


## Make deliverables specific enough to compare


Do not stop at a post count. Ask what kind of draft is included, how many options you receive, whether revisions are included, and which formats are in scope. A thoughtful founder post, a customer-story post, a technical explanation, and a company announcement can require different inputs and review.


Define the output in plain language. For example, a scoped engagement might identify the expected number of LinkedIn drafts, the source material for each, the review window, and whether an editorial calendar is included. It should also say what happens when new requests fall outside that plan.


Rethoric's guide to[LinkedIn content management for founders](https://www.rethoric.com/blog-posts/linkedin-content-management-for-founders) is useful context here: content needs a working path from source to approval, not just a file full of drafts.


## Price the approval process honestly


Founder approval is part of the cost of the work, even when it is not listed as a line item. A fast, focused review protects accuracy and voice. An unowned review process can delay every draft, create contradictory feedback, and make cadence impossible to predict.


Ask who consolidates feedback, how many revision rounds are included, who gives final approval, and what happens when a draft needs legal, product, or customer review. Those answers make the proposal more useful than an abstract promise of unlimited revisions.


The goal is not to minimize founder involvement. It is to reserve it for the decisions only the founder can make: what is true, what is defensible, and what is worth saying publicly.


## Decide whether strategy and distribution are in scope


Some founders need help producing posts. Others need a clearer point of view, a topic backlog, a review rhythm, and a plan for getting useful ideas in front of the right people. Treat those as separate questions when you compare pricing.


Strategy can include defining the intended audience, recurring themes, and the role each post should play. Distribution can include practical support around publishing or engagement. Neither should be implied by the word ghostwriting. Ask for the operating responsibilities in writing.


If you are deciding whether to build internally or buy help, Rethoric's[LinkedIn content team guide](https://www.rethoric.com/blog-posts/linkedin-content-team-for-founders) can help frame the ownership question. A provider is easier to evaluate when the internal responsibilities are equally clear.


## Watch for comparisons that hide tradeoffs


A proposal becomes difficult to compare when it relies on broad promises: thought leadership, authority, viral posts, or inbound. Those outcomes depend on the founder's expertise, the audience, timing, the quality of the source material, and many decisions outside a writing engagement.


Ask the provider to replace broad language with a description of the work they control. A credible scope can explain how they gather material, draft it, check claims, manage feedback, and report what they observed. It should not promise that a fixed number of posts will produce a fixed business result.


Also look for exclusions. Design, profile updates, comments, employee advocacy, paid distribution, executive coaching, and analytics can all be valuable. They are simply different services that may need a separate owner and budget.


## Use a proposal scorecard before you choose


A short scorecard keeps price from becoming the only decision criterion. Review each proposal against the same questions:


-


Does the source process make it plausible that the content will reflect the founder's real experience?


-


Are deliverables, revision boundaries, and turnaround assumptions explicit?


-


Is there a named owner for approval and factual review?


-


Are strategy, publishing, and distribution clearly included or excluded?


-


Can the provider explain how they will handle information that should not be public?


-


Is the first review point defined so both sides can adjust the workflow?


Then compare the tradeoffs. A lean engagement may be ideal when you already have a content lead and reliable source material. A more managed engagement may fit when the founder needs help converting a busy operating week into a consistent editorial process. The right answer is the scope that matches the bottleneck you actually have.


## Plan the first month as a learning period


The first month should test the workflow, not prove a dramatic outcome. Use it to learn whether the source conversations reveal useful material, whether the drafts sound like the founder, how quickly approvals happen, and which topics deserve another pass.


Keep a short record of what changed: the topics explored, feedback that improved accuracy, delays in the approval path, and questions from the market that could become future content. That creates a better basis for changing the scope than engagement totals alone.


For a broader view of the practice, see Rethoric's[ghostwriting for founders guide](https://www.rethoric.com/blog-posts/ghostwriting-for-founders) . It explains the role of a repeatable content engine without treating the founder's voice as something a tool can replace.


## Choose clarity over a headline price


LinkedIn ghostwriting pricing should tell you what work is being done, who owns each decision, and where the relationship stops. When those answers are explicit, a founder can compare proposals on fit rather than on a number stripped of its context.
